newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court rejects plea by man facing sterilization.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court rejects plea by man facing sterilization.

text.p: A federal appeals court ruled on Friday that an illegal immigrant from China was not entitled to political asylum in the United States because of China's policy of limiting couples to a single child.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an appeal by De You Chen, who fled to the United States in 1993 when Chinese authorities ordered him to be sterilized after he and his wife had a third child in violation of China's birth control policy of one child per couple.

The court ruled that, to be eligible for asylum, an immigrant had to show evidence of persecution for reasons other than general population control, such as different treatment for those who publicly opposed the policy.

"Chen's only acts relevant to his political opposition to the PRC's (People's Republic of China) birth control policies were his violation of the policies to explain that he wanted a son. Neither of these acts constituted political expression," the court's ruling said.
"There was no indication that the PRC was motivated by Chen's political opinions," it added.
After entering the United States illegally, Chen applied for political asylum and withholding of deportation on the basis of his political opinions.

But an immigration judge denied Chen's application, citing an earlier ruling that China's family planning policies do not constitute grounds for political asylum. The Board of Immigration Appeals and a U.S. District Court both rejected Chen's appeals.
Chen appealed to the Appeals Court, maintaining that the legal ruling relied upon by the immigration judge had been overruled by administrative action and by an executive order.

Officials in President George Bush's administration proposed immigration rules that would have given refugee status to people facing forced abortion or sterilization, but the rules were never officially adopted, the Appeals Court said.

A 1990 executive order signed by Bush ordering officials to give greater consideration to immigrants who feared persecution because of a country's policy of forced sterilization lacked legal force because it was not backed up by statute, the court said in rejecting Chen's appeal.

After Chen and his wife Lan-Zheng Sun had a second daughter, Chinese authorities fined them and ordered Sun to be implanted with an intra-uterine device. Because the couple wanted a boy, they had the device illegally removed and in 1990, Sun became pregnant again.
"Upon learning of her pregnancy, the authorities threatened to destroy the couple's home if she did not abort the child," the court ruling said.

The couple fled to a nearby village and the authorities did destroy their home, it said. After Sun gave birth to a boy, authorities scheduled her for sterilization. Because she was too ill for surgery, the authorities ordered that Chen be sterilized instead, the ruling said. Chen fled to California, where he was arrested.
